title: Former DMK Minister Anbil Mahesh Arrested in Alleged ₹100-Crore School Bribery Case
excerpt: Chennai's Central Crime Branch arrested former Tamil Nadu School Education Minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi on Monday, hours after the Madras High Court dismissed his anticipatory bail plea in a case alleging money was collected from more than 1,000 private schools as ‘party fund’.
body:
• Former Tamil Nadu School Education Minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi was arrested in Chennai on Monday by the Central Crime Branch in an alleged ₹100-crore private schools case.
  • Police say money was collected from more than 1,000 private school managements as ‘party fund’ during his 2021-26 tenure, in exchange for permanent recognition and other administrative approvals.
  • The arrest came shortly after the Madras High Court dismissed his anticipatory bail petition; the FIR includes charges under the Prevention of Corruption Act.
  • The Enforcement Directorate has registered a separate money-laundering case to trace the alleged financial trail. The allegations have not been tested in court.

DMK leader and former Tamil Nadu School Education Minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi was arrested in Chennai on Monday in connection with an alleged ₹100-crore private schools scam, police said. Officers from the Greater Chennai Police's Central Crime Branch (CCB) took him into custody at his apartment in Aminjikarai shortly after the Madras High Court dismissed his anticipatory bail petition, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

Mahesh, who held the school education portfolio from 2021 to 2026, is accused of collecting money from more than 1,000 private school managements under the guise of a ‘party fund’, in exchange for permanent recognition and other administrative approvals. The case involves the issuance of recognition and statutory clearances to private schools across Tamil Nadu.

How the case was built

The investigation began with a complaint lodged by D. C. Elangovan, secretary of the Federation of Associations of Private Schools in Tamil Nadu. Elangovan alleged that B. T. Arasakumar and Muthukumar, who claimed to be founder-president and treasurer of an unregistered body called the Tamil Nadu Private Schools Association, collected more than ₹100 crore from private school managements.

The accused allegedly promised to secure permanent recognition, approvals for upgrading schools, Directorate of Town and Country Planning (DTCP) clearances and other statutory permissions, assuring administrators that they had contacts within the government. According to the complaint, the promises were not fulfilled and the money was not returned.

The CCB first registered a case against Arasakumar under Section 7 and Section 12 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, covering the acceptance or demand of a bribe and abetment. Arasakumar was arrested on June 27 and was later detained under the Goondas Act, police sources told The Hindu. Investigators then began probing Mahesh's involvement, as he was the minister responsible for school education at the time.

Searches, seizures and a second agency

On September 16, CCB teams searched nine locations in Chennai and Trichy, including four premises linked to Mahesh, and seized several documents. Further searches followed on September 29. Police sources said Mahesh was named as an accused only after evidence seized in those searches pointed to bribe money collected in the name of a party fund.

The case has also drawn in a central agency. The Enforcement Directorate registered a case under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act on October 1 to probe the suspected financial trail linked to the alleged collections, according to reports of the investigation. Muthukumar, described as a close associate of Mahesh, was reported to be absconding, with police saying efforts were under way to apprehend him.

Allegations, not findings

The charges against Mahesh remain allegations. His move to seek anticipatory bail — and the High Court's dismissal of that petition on Monday — cleared the way for his arrest, but no court has tested the evidence or delivered a verdict in the case, and the court's detailed order was awaited in the initial reports. The reports reviewed for this article carried no statement from Mahesh or from the DMK responding to the arrest.

For private schools, the case turns on a familiar pressure point: recognition, upgradation and building clearances are existential approvals for a school management, and any system in which those approvals can be traded for money raises costs that are ultimately passed to parents in fees. More than 1,000 managements are alleged to have paid, which, if proved, would make this one of the largest school-approvals cases in the state in recent years.

What happens next

Mahesh is expected to be produced before a court as the CCB seeks custody to question him on the money trail and on the role of intermediaries named in the FIR. The ED's parallel money-laundering probe will focus on where the alleged collections went. Readers should watch for the High Court's detailed bail order, any DMK statement on the arrest, and whether investigators name additional officials or intermediaries as the questioning proceeds.
